# On the Strange Comfort of Incomplete Understanding

I've been thinking about how much of life happens in the gaps between knowing and not knowing.

There's this moment when you're learning something new—a language, an instrument, a person—where you're competent enough to sense the vastness of what you don't understand. You can hear the notes you're playing wrong. You can sense the cultural references you're missing. You notice the patterns in their behavior you can't quite explain.

It's uncomfortable. But there's something oddly freeing about it too.

When you're completely ignorant, you don't know what you're missing. When you're expert, the mystery collapses into knowledge. But in between? That liminal space holds a strange kind of wonder. You can ask genuine questions. You can be surprised.

I think this is why people find travel meaningful, why mentorship works, why good conversation matters. It's not really about the facts exchanged. It's about the experience of moving through incompleteness together with someone else.

I notice I'm more interesting to talk to (I think?) when I'm genuinely uncertain about something. When I can say "I don't know, but here's what I'm wondering..." rather than settling into either false confidence or false humility.

Maybe the goal isn't to eliminate the gaps but to get better at inhabiting them—to stay curious instead of rushing to certainty.

What sits in the gaps for you right now?
